chapter: Lover Man and the postwar years
title: Harlem social life and dance work in the Fifties
summary: He could work forty weeks a year at Harlem and out-of-town Black clubs, the Renaissance, Small's, Saratoga and the Savoy's last stage.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: At this time, the sort of night-life of Harlem had changed, hadn't it.

Oh yes! I mean, in those years... I mean, I could work forty weeks out of the year, not only in Harlem, but in Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington, Sioux City, Iowa. In colored places, especially on Sunday, when people dressed on Sunday and came out... I mean, it was a different lifestyles in those years than it is today. People dressed to go out! You know what I mean? They don't do that any more. And then, you had different dances, sororities, different college fraternities... I mean, they didn't have to go downtown to mingle with the White people. They used to come up to Harlem, or go anywhere, because those dancers were great! And they were pretty wild(?) then.

I don't know, things have changed so much. I could work in the Renaissance alone in Harlem, and fill out a
week; various clubs that gave dances there...
If you played the Renaissance, what...
Yeah, but what sort of group did you have in there?
A little band, a regular group, you know.
The Royal Tea Room. Saratoga Club on Lenox Avenue.
Did the Saratoga still continue to operate?
No, I don't think they... They continued it under another name. And then the Savoy, of course, was open for... This was maybe the last stage of the Savoy, in the Fifties, wasn't it?
Let me see. Yes, it is, because... The last time I was there, Cootie Williams was there with eight pieces and an organ player. You know, it was all...
